chapters.title: Nǐ Hǎo — Hello, Character by Character
chapters.label: ch:zh-nihao
chapters.canDo: I can greet someone in Mandarin and answer when greeted, reading both characters unaided and saying the greeting with the tone a speaker actually uses rather than the one the dictionary prints.

payoff.summary: A two-line meeting in which both voices say the same word — read from the characters alone, with the first third tone raised by sandhi.

chapters.title: Reading the Greeting — One Piece at a Time
chapters.label: ch:zh-components
chapters.canDo: I can write each component the greeting's two characters are built from, and then assemble both characters from those pieces rather than recalling them as whole shapes.

payoff.summary: The second assembly, built from two components the reader wrote individually a moment earlier — and a caution that the memorable story about why it means what it means is a story, not a source.

chapters.title: One to Five — Where the Character Is the Count
chapters.label: ch:zh-numbers
chapters.canDo: I can count from one to five in Mandarin and read all five characters cold and out of order, and I know which of them I could have worked out and which I simply had to learn.

payoff.summary: The five numerals read out of sequence, then off a lift panel with the fourth floor missing — and the reader knows why it is missing.

chapters.title: One Box, Two Characters, and the First Thing You Can Refuse
chapters.label: ch:zh-negation
chapters.canDo: I can write 口 and 日 -- the second being the first with one bar added -- and I can disagree in Mandarin by putting 不 in front of a word I already know, because Mandarin has no standalone word for no.

payoff.summary: The first exchange in the book that contains a disagreement -- a greeting, a question, and a refusal built by negating a word the reader has had since the opening lesson.

chapters.title: Yes, No, and a Tone That Moves
chapters.label: ch:zh-shi
chapters.canDo: I can write 是 by finishing 日 before the body underneath, answer a yes-or-no question either way by keeping or negating the word I was asked about, and apply the rule that 不 rises before a falling tone even though the writing never shows it.

payoff.summary: The first exchange in which the reader can answer either way -- 是 for yes, 不是 for no -- and hear the negator's pitch rise on a page that records no such thing.

chapters.title: See You Again
chapters.label: ch:zh-zaijian
chapters.canDo: I can write 再 and 见, say goodbye with 再见, read the word literally as "see again" because its two pieces genuinely add up, and name which expressions I know are spoken differently from how they are written.

payoff.summary: The first exchange in the track that opens, turns and closes -- greeting, an answer either way, and a parting -- with every line built from characters the reader has written rather than a phrase memorised whole.

chapters.title: Good Morning, and a Rule That Declines to Fire
chapters.label: ch:zh-zaoshang
chapters.canDo: I can write 早 and 上, greet someone with 早上好, hear a neutral-tone syllable as the absence of a tone mark rather than a mistake, and say why the third-tone rule changes 你好 but leaves 早上好 alone.

payoff.summary: The first exchange where the reader chooses between two correct greetings rather than reciting the only one available -- and the first place all three tone behaviours in the track line up side by side, one moving and two declining to.

chapters.title: Saying Who You Are
chapters.label: ch:zh-mingzi
chapters.canDo: I can write 我, 名 and 字, introduce myself with 我是 and my own name, recognise 名字 as the word for a name, and I know that Mandarin words never change shape for grammar.

payoff.summary: The first exchange the reader cannot finish without supplying something of their own -- their name -- and the first place the book names a gap it is choosing not to fill, rather than teaching a sentence no speaker would say.
